claim: Floral abscission is controlled by the leucine-rich repeat receptor kinase (LRR-RK) HAESA and the peptide hormone IDA.
source: Floral abscission is controlled by the leucine-rich repeat receptor kinase (LRR-RK) HAESA and the peptide hormone IDA.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a known fact about the floral abscission pathway.

claim: IDA is sensed directly by the HAESA ectodomain.
source: Here we show that IDA is sensed directly by the HAESA ectodomain.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by experimental data including ITC and crystal structures.

claim: The HAESA hormone binding pocket accommodates an active dodecamer peptide.
source: Crystal structures of HAESA in complex with IDA reveal a hormone binding pocket that accommodates an active dodecamer peptide.
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data presented in the manuscript.

claim: A central hydroxyproline residue anchors IDA to the receptor.
source: A central hydroxyproline residue anchors IDA to the receptor.
evidence: This is supported by structural data showing the interaction between Hyp64 and HAESA.

claim: SERK1 is a positive regulator of the floral abscission pathway.
source: The HAESA co-receptor SERK1, a positive regulator of the floral abscission pathway, allows for high-affinity sensing of the peptide hormone by binding to an Arg-His-Asn motif in IDA.
evidence: This is supported by genetic and biochemical data including petal break-strength assays and ITC experiments.

claim: SERK1 allows for high-affinity sensing of the peptide hormone by binding to an Arg-His-Asn motif in IDA.
source: The HAESA co-receptor SERK1, a positive regulator of the floral abscission pathway, allows for high-affinity sensing of the peptide hormone by binding to an Arg-His-Asn motif in IDA.
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data and ITC measurements showing increased binding affinity.

claim: The Arg-His-Asn sequence pattern is conserved among diverse plant peptides.
source: This sequence pattern is conserved among diverse plant peptides, suggesting that plant peptide hormone receptors may share a common ligand binding mode and activation mechanism.
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 7.

claim: Plant peptide hormone receptors may share a common ligand binding mode and activation mechanism.
source: This sequence pattern is conserved among diverse plant peptides, suggesting that plant peptide hormone receptors may share a common ligand binding mode and activation mechanism.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the conservation of the Arg-His-Asn motif across different peptide families.

claim: HAESA and HAESA-LIKE 2 (HSL2) redundantly control floral abscission.
source: The LRR-RKs HAESA (greek: to adhere to) and HAESA-LIKE 2 (HSL2) redundantly control floral abscission (Cho et al., 2008; Jinn et al., 2000; Stenvik et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Loss-of-function of IDA causes floral organs to remain attached.
source: Loss-of-function of the secreted small protein INFLORESCENCE DEFICIENT IN ABSCISSION (IDA) causes floral organs to remain attached while its over-expression leads to premature shedding (Butenko et al., 2003; Stenvik et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Over-expression of IDA leads to premature shedding of floral organs.
source: Loss-of-function of the secreted small protein INFLORESCENCE DEFICIENT IN ABSCISSION (IDA) causes floral organs to remain attached while its over-expression leads to premature shedding (Butenko et al., 2003; Stenvik et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Full-length IDA is proteolytically processed.
source: Full-length IDA is proteolytically processed and a conserved stretch of 20 amino-acids (termed EPIP) can rescue the IDA loss-of-function phenotype (Figure 1A) (Stenvik et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: A conserved stretch of 20 amino-acids (termed EPIP) can rescue the IDA loss-of-function phenotype.
source: Full-length IDA is proteolytically processed and a conserved stretch of 20 amino-acids (termed EPIP) can rescue the IDA loss-of-function phenotype (Figure 1A) (Stenvik et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: A dodecamer peptide within EPIP is able to activate HAESA and HSL2 in transient assays in tobacco cells.
source: It has been demonstrated that a dodecamer peptide within EPIP is able to activate HAESA and HSL2 in transient assays in tobacco cells (Butenko et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The dodecamer sequence motif in IDA contains a central Pro residue, presumed to be post-translationally modified to hydroxyproline.
source: This sequence motif is highly conserved among IDA family members (IDA-LIKE PROTEINS, IDLs) and contains a central Pro residue, presumed to be post-translationally modified to hydroxyproline (Hyp; Figure 1A) (Butenko et al., 2003; 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: IDA binds to HAESA with a dissociation constant (Kd) of approximately 20 μM.
source: A Hyp-modified dodecamer comprising the highly conserved PIP motif in IDA (Figure 1A) interacts with HAESA with 1:1 stoichiometry (N) and with a dissociation constant (Kd) of ~20 μM (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: IDA binds to HAESA with 1:1 stoichiometry.
source: A Hyp-modified dodecamer comprising the highly conserved PIP motif in IDA (Figure 1A) interacts with HAESA with 1:1 stoichiometry (N) and with a dissociation constant (Kd) of ~20 μM (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The structure of the apo HAESA ectodomain was determined at 1.74 Å resolution.
source: We next determined crystal structures of the apo HAESA ectodomain and of a HAESA-IDA complex, at 1.74 and 1.86 Å resolution, respectively (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D; Tables 1,2).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data in Table 1.

claim: The structure of the HAESA-IDA complex was determined at 1.86 Å resolution.
source: We next determined crystal structures of the apo HAESA ectodomain and of a HAESA-IDA complex, at 1.74 and 1.86 Å resolution, respectively (Figure 1C; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–D; Tables 1,2).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data in Table 2.

claim: IDA binds in a completely extended conformation along the inner surface of the HAESA ectodomain.
source: IDA binds in a completely extended conformation along the inner surface of the HAESA ectodomain, covering LRRs 2–14 (Figure 1C,D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: IDA binding covers HAESA LRRs 2–14.
source: IDA binds in a completely extended conformation along the inner surface of the HAESA ectodomain, covering LRRs 2–14 (Figure 1C,D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: The central Hyp64IDA is buried in a specific pocket formed by HAESA LRRs 8–10.
source: The central Hyp64IDA is buried in a specific pocket formed by HAESA LRRs 8–10, with its hydroxyl group establishing hydrogen bonds with the strictly conserved Glu266HAESA and with a water molecule, which in turn is coordinated by the main chain oxygens of Phe289HAESA and Ser311HAESA (Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The hydroxyl group of Hyp64IDA establishes hydrogen bonds with Glu266HAESA and a water molecule.
source: The central Hyp64IDA is buried in a specific pocket formed by HAESA LRRs 8–10, with its hydroxyl group establishing hydrogen bonds with the strictly conserved Glu266HAESA and with a water molecule, which in turn is coordinated by the main chain oxygens of Phe289HAESA and Ser311HAESA (Figure 1E; Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: IDA does not require arabinosylation of Hyp64IDA for activity in vivo.
source: The restricted size of the Hyp pocket suggests that IDA does not require arabinosylation of Hyp64IDA for activity in vivo, a modification that has been reported for Hyp residues in plant CLE peptide hormones (Ohyama et al., 2009).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observation of the restricted size of the Hyp pocket.

claim: The C-terminal Arg-His-Asn motif in IDA maps to a cavity formed by HAESA LRRs 11–14.
source: The C-terminal Arg-His-Asn motif in IDA maps to a cavity formed by HAESA LRRs 11–14 (Figure 1D,F).
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 1D and 1F.

claim: The COO- group of Asn69IDA is in direct contact with Arg407HAESA and Arg409HAESA.
source: The COO- group of Asn69IDA is in direct contact with Arg407HAESA and Arg409HAESA and HAESA cannot bind a C-terminally extended IDA-SFVN peptide (Figures 1D,F, 2D).
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data shown in Figures 1D, 1F, and 2D.

claim: HAESA cannot bind a C-terminally extended IDA-SFVN peptide.
source: The COO- group of Asn69IDA is in direct contact with Arg407HAESA and Arg409HAESA and HAESA cannot bind a C-terminally extended IDA-SFVN peptide (Figures 1D,F, 2D).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The conserved Asn69IDA may constitute the very C-terminus of the mature IDA peptide in planta.
source: This suggests that the conserved Asn69IDA may constitute the very C-terminus of the mature IDA peptide in planta and that active IDA is generated by proteolytic processing from a longer pre-protein (Stenvik et al., 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observation that HAESA cannot bind C-terminally extended IDA.

claim: Active IDA is generated by proteolytic processing from a longer pre-protein.
source: This suggests that the conserved Asn69IDA may constitute the very C-terminus of the mature IDA peptide in planta and that active IDA is generated by proteolytic processing from a longer pre-protein (Stenvik et al., 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from structural data and supported by citation.

claim: Mutation of Arg417HSL2 causes a loss-of-function phenotype in HSL2.
source: Mutation of Arg417HSL2 (which corresponds to Arg409HAESA) causes a loss-of-function phenotype in HSL2, which indicates that the peptide binding pockets in different HAESA receptors have common structural and sequence features (Niederhuth et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The peptide binding pockets in different HAESA receptors have common structural and sequence features.
source: Mutation of Arg417HSL2 (which corresponds to Arg409HAESA) causes a loss-of-function phenotype in HSL2, which indicates that the peptide binding pockets in different HAESA receptors have common structural and sequence features (Niederhuth et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the functional consequence of the mutation and supported by citation.

claim: Many residues contributing to the formation of the IDA binding surface in HAESA are conserved in HSL2 and in other HAESA-type receptors in different plant species.
source: Indeed, we find many of the residues contributing to the formation of the IDA binding surface in HAESA to be conserved in HSL2 and in other HAESA-type receptors in different plant species (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: A N-terminal Pro-rich motif in IDA makes contacts with LRRs 2–6 of the receptor.
source: A N-terminal Pro-rich motif in IDA makes contacts with LRRs 2–6 of the receptor (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the HAESA-PKGV-IDA structure, no additional electron density accounts for the PKGV motif at the IDA N-terminus.
source: In this structure, no additional electron density accounts for the PKGV motif at the IDA N-terminus (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: PKGV-IDA and IDA have similar binding affinities.
source: Consistently, PKGV-IDA and IDA have similar binding affinities in our ITC assays, further indicating that HAESA senses a dodecamer peptide comprising residues 58-69IDA (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: HAESA senses a dodecamer peptide comprising residues 58-69IDA.
source: Consistently, PKGV-IDA and IDA have similar binding affinities in our ITC assays, further indicating that HAESA senses a dodecamer peptide comprising residues 58-69IDA (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is inferred from the similar binding affinities of IDA and PKGV-IDA.

claim: IDL1 can rescue IDA loss-of-function mutants when introduced in abscission zone cells.
source: IDL1, which can rescue IDA loss-of-function mutants when introduced in abscission zone cells, can also be sensed by HAESA, albeit with lower affinity (Figure 2D) (Stenvik et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: IDL1 can be sensed by HAESA, albeit with lower affinity than IDA.
source: IDL1, which can rescue IDA loss-of-function mutants when introduced in abscission zone cells, can also be sensed by HAESA, albeit with lower affinity (Figure 2D) (Stenvik et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Different IDA family members use a common binding mode to interact with HAESA-type receptors.
source: A 2.56 Å co-crystal structure with IDL1 reveals that different IDA family members use a common binding mode to interact with HAESA-type receptors (Stenvik et al., 2008; Butenko et al., 2009) (Figure 2A–C,E, Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 2A-C and 2E.

claim: HAESA does not detect interaction with a synthetic peptide missing the C-terminal Asn69IDA (ΔN69).
source: We do not detect interaction between HAESA and a synthetic peptide missing the C-terminal Asn69IDA (ΔN69), highlighting the importance of the polar interactions between the IDA carboxy-terminus and Arg407HAESA/Arg409HAESA (Figures 1F, 2D).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Replacing Hyp64IDA with proline impairs the interaction with the receptor.
source: Replacing Hyp64IDA, which is common to all IDLs, with proline impairs the interaction with the receptor, as does the Lys66IDA/Arg67IDA → Ala double-mutant discussed below (Figure 1A, 2D).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The Lys66IDA/Arg67IDA → Ala double-mutant impairs the interaction with the receptor.
source: Replacing Hyp64IDA, which is common to all IDLs, with proline impairs the interaction with the receptor, as does the Lys66IDA/Arg67IDA → Ala double-mutant discussed below (Figure 1A, 2D).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: HAESA can discriminate between IDLs and functionally unrelated dodecamer peptides with Hyp modifications, such as CLV3.
source: Notably, HAESA can discriminate between IDLs and functionally unrelated dodecamer peptides with Hyp modifications, such as CLV3 (Figures 2D, 7) (Ogawa et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 2D and sequence alignment in Figure 7.

claim: SOMATIC EMBRYOGENESIS RECEPTOR KINASES (SERKs) are positive regulators of floral abscission.
source: It has been recently reported that SOMATIC EMBRYOGENESIS RECEPTOR KINASES (SERKs) are positive regulators of floral abscission and can interact with HAESA and HSL2 in an IDA-dependent manner (Meng et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: SERKs can interact with HAESA and HSL2 in an IDA-dependent manner.
source: It has been recently reported that SOMATIC EMBRYOGENESIS RECEPTOR KINASES (SERKs) are positive regulators of floral abscission and can interact with HAESA and HSL2 in an IDA-dependent manner (Meng et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work.

claim: All five SERK family members appear to be expressed in the Arabidopsis abscission zone.
source: As all five SERK family members appear to be expressed in the Arabidopsis abscission zone (Niederhuth et al., 2013), we quantified their relative contribution to floral abscission in Arabidopsis using a petal break-strength assay (Lease et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Among the SERK family members, SERK1 is a positive regulator of floral abscission.
source: Our experiments suggest that among the SERK family members, SERK1 is a positive regulator of floral abscission.
evidence: This is supported by petal break-strength assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The force required to remove the petals of serk1-1 mutants is significantly higher than that needed for wild-type plants.
source: We found that the force required to remove the petals of serk1-1 mutants is significantly higher than that needed for wild-type plants, as previously observed for haesa/hsl2 mutants (Stenvik et al., 2008), and that floral abscission is delayed in serk1-1 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by petal break-strength assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Floral abscission is delayed in serk1-1.
source: We found that the force required to remove the petals of serk1-1 mutants is significantly higher than that needed for wild-type plants, as previously observed for haesa/hsl2 mutants (Stenvik et al., 2008), and that floral abscission is delayed in serk1-1 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by petal break-strength assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: The serk2-2, serk3-1, serk4-1 and serk5-1 mutant lines showed a petal break-strength profile not significantly different from wild-type plants.
source: The serk2-2, serk3-1, serk4-1 and serk5-1 mutant lines (Albrecht et al., 2008) showed a petal break-strength profile not significantly different from wild-type plants.
evidence: This is supported by petal break-strength assay data.

claim: The LRR ectodomain of SERK1 forms stable, IDA-dependent heterodimeric complexes with HAESA in vitro.
source: In vitro, the LRR ectodomain of SERK1 (residues 24–213) forms stable, IDA-dependent heterodimeric complexes with HAESA in size exclusion chromatography experiments (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: HAESA senses IDA with a ~60 fold higher binding affinity in the presence of SERK1.
source: We found that HAESA senses IDA with a ~60 fold higher binding affinity in the presence of SERK1, suggesting that SERK1 is involved in the specific recognition of the peptide hormone (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: SERK1 is involved in the specific recognition of the peptide hormone IDA.
source: We found that HAESA senses IDA with a ~60 fold higher binding affinity in the presence of SERK1, suggesting that SERK1 is involved in the specific recognition of the peptide hormone (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is inferred from the increased binding affinity observed in ITC experiments.

claim: There is no detectable interaction between HAESA and SERK1 in the absence of IDA.
source: We next titrated SERK1 into a solution containing only the HAESA ectodomain. In this case, there was no detectable interaction between receptor and co-receptor, while in the presence of IDA, SERK1 strongly binds HAESA with a dissociation constant in the mid-nanomolar range (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: In the presence of IDA, SERK1 strongly binds HAESA with a dissociation constant in the mid-nanomolar range.
source: We next titrated SERK1 into a solution containing only the HAESA ectodomain. In this case, there was no detectable interaction between receptor and co-receptor, while in the presence of IDA, SERK1 strongly binds HAESA with a dissociation constant in the mid-nanomolar range (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: IDA itself promotes receptor – co-receptor association.
source: This suggests that IDA itself promotes receptor – co-receptor association, as previously described for the steroid hormone brassinolide (Santiago et al., 2013) and for other LRR-RK complexes (Sun et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is inferred from the ITC data and supported by citations to similar mechanisms in other systems.

claim: Hydroxyprolination of IDA is critical for HAESA-IDA-SERK1 complex formation.
source: Importantly, hydroxyprolination of IDA is critical for HAESA-IDA-SERK1 complex formation (Figure 3C,D).
evidence: This is supported by ITC and size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 3C and 3D.

claim: SERKs may render HAESA, and potentially other receptor kinases, competent for high-affinity sensing of their cognate ligands.
source: Our calorimetry experiments now reveal that SERKs may render HAESA, and potentially other receptor kinases, competent for high-affinity sensing of their cognate ligands.
evidence: This is inferred from the ITC data showing increased binding affinity in the presence of SERK1.

claim: The HAESA kinase domain can transphosphorylate SERK1 in vitro.
source: Consistently, the HAESA kinase domain can transphosphorylate SERK1 and vice versa in in vitro transphosphorylation assays (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The SERK1 kinase domain can transphosphorylate HAESA in vitro.
source: Consistently, the HAESA kinase domain can transphosphorylate SERK1 and vice versa in in vitro transphosphorylation assays (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro kinase assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: SERK1 is a HAESA co-receptor in the Arabidopsis abscission zone.
source: Together, our genetic and biochemical experiments implicate SERK1 as a HAESA co-receptor in the Arabidopsis abscission zone.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined genetic and biochemical data presented in the study.

claim: A 2.43 Å crystal structure of the ternary HAESA – IDA – SERK1 complex was solved.
source: To understand in molecular terms how SERK1 contributes to high-affinity IDA recognition, we solved a 2.43 Å crystal structure of the ternary HAESA – IDA – SERK1 complex (Figure 4A, Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by crystallographic data in Table 2.

claim: HAESA LRRs 16–21 and its C-terminal capping domain undergo a conformational change upon SERK1 binding.
source: HAESA LRRs 16–21 and its C-terminal capping domain undergo a conformational change upon SERK1 binding (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The SERK1 ectodomain interacts with the IDA peptide binding site using a loop region (residues 51-59SERK1) from its N-terminal cap.
source: The SERK1 ectodomain interacts with the IDA peptide binding site using a loop region (residues 51-59SERK1) from its N-terminal cap (Figure 4A,C).
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 4A and 4C.

claim: SERK1 loop residues establish multiple hydrophobic and polar contacts with Lys66IDA and the C-terminal Arg-His-Asn motif in IDA.
source: SERK1 loop residues establish multiple hydrophobic and polar contacts with Lys66IDA and the C-terminal Arg-His-Asn motif in IDA (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: SERK1 LRRs 1–5 and its C-terminal capping domain form an additional zipper-like interface with residues originating from HAESA LRRs 15–21 and from the HAESA C-terminal cap.
source: SERK1 LRRs 1–5 and its C-terminal capping domain form an additional zipper-like interface with residues originating from HAESA LRRs 15–21 and from the HAESA C-terminal cap (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: SERK1 binds HAESA using two distinct interaction surfaces.
source: SERK1 binds HAESA using these two distinct interaction surfaces (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), with the N-cap of the SERK1 LRR domain partially covering the IDA peptide binding cleft.
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The N-cap of the SERK1 LRR domain partially covers the IDA peptide binding cleft.
source: SERK1 binds HAESA using these two distinct interaction surfaces (Figure 1—figure supplement 3), with the N-cap of the SERK1 LRR domain partially covering the IDA peptide binding cleft.
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data.

claim: SERK1 recognizes a C-terminal Arg-His-Asn motif in IDA.
source: Our experiments reveal that SERK1 recognizes a C-terminal Arg-His-Asn motif in IDA.
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data showing direct contacts between SERK1 and this motif.

claim: The C-terminal Arg-His-Asn motif can be found in other peptide hormone families.
source: Importantly, this motif can also be found in other peptide hormone families (Kondo et al., 2006; Matsuzaki et al., 2010; Tang et al., 2015) (Figure 7).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 7 and citations.

claim: CLEs in their mature form are hydroxyprolinated dodecamers.
source: It is interesting to note, that CLEs in their mature form are also hydroxyprolinated dodecamers, which bind to a surface area in the BARELY ANY MERISTEM 1 receptor that would correspond to part of the IDA binding cleft in HAESA (Kondo et al., 2006; Ogawa et al., 2008; Shinohara et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: CLEs bind to a surface area in the BARELY ANY MERISTEM 1 receptor that would correspond to part of the IDA binding cleft in HAESA.
source: It is interesting to note, that CLEs in their mature form are also hydroxyprolinated dodecamers, which bind to a surface area in the BARELY ANY MERISTEM 1 receptor that would correspond to part of the IDA binding cleft in HAESA (Kondo et al., 2006; Ogawa et al., 2008; Shinohara et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work and structural comparison.

claim: Diverse plant peptide hormones may bind their LRR-RK receptors in an extended conformation along the inner surface of the LRR domain.
source: Diverse plant peptide hormones may thus also bind their LRR-RK receptors in an extended conformation along the inner surface of the LRR domain and may also use small, shape-complementary co-receptors for high-affinity ligand binding and receptor activation.
evidence: This is speculated based on the structural similarities observed between IDA and CLE binding modes.

claim: Diverse plant peptide hormones may use small, shape-complementary co-receptors for high-affinity ligand binding and receptor activation.
source: Diverse plant peptide hormones may thus also bind their LRR-RK receptors in an extended conformation along the inner surface of the LRR domain and may also use small, shape-complementary co-receptors for high-affinity ligand binding and receptor activation.
evidence: This is speculated based on the role of SERK1 in the HAESA-IDA system.

claim: Deletion of the buried Asn69IDA completely inhibits receptor – co-receptor complex formation.
source: Deletion of the buried Asn69IDA completely inhibits receptor – co-receptor complex formation and HSL2 activation (Figure 5A,B) (Butenko et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by size exclusion chromatography data shown in Figure 5A and citation.

claim: Deletion of the buried Asn69IDA inhibits HSL2 activation.
source: Deletion of the buried Asn69IDA completely inhibits receptor – co-receptor complex formation and HSL2 activation (Figure 5A,B) (Butenko et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: A synthetic Lys66IDA/Arg67IDA → Ala mutant peptide showed a 10 fold reduced binding affinity when titrated in a HAESA/SERK1 protein solution.
source: A synthetic Lys66IDA/Arg67IDA → Ala mutant peptide (IDA K66A/R66A) showed a 10 fold reduced binding affinity when titrated in a HAESA/SERK1 protein solution (Figures 5A,B, 2D).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Over-expression of wild-type IDA leads to early floral abscission and an enlargement of the abscission zone.
source: We found that over-expression of wild-type IDA leads to early floral abscission and an enlargement of the abscission zone (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This is supported by petal break-strength assay data and images shown in Figure 5C-E.

claim: Over-expression of the IDA Lys66IDA/Arg67IDA → Ala double mutant significantly delays floral abscission when compared to wild-type control plants.
source: In contrast, over-expression of the IDA Lys66IDA/Arg67IDA → Ala double mutant significantly delays floral abscission when compared to wild-type control plants, suggesting that the mutant IDA peptide has reduced activity in planta (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This is supported by petal break-strength assay data shown in Figure 5C-E.

claim: The mutant IDA peptide (Lys66IDA/Arg67IDA → Ala) has reduced activity in planta.
source: In contrast, over-expression of the IDA Lys66IDA/Arg67IDA → Ala double mutant significantly delays floral abscission when compared to wild-type control plants, suggesting that the mutant IDA peptide has reduced activity in planta (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This is inferred from the delayed abscission phenotype observed in the mutant.

claim: Mutation of Lys66IDA/Arg67IDA → Ala may cause a weak dominant negative effect.
source: Comparison of 35S::IDA wild-type and mutant plants further indicates that mutation of Lys66IDA/Arg67IDA → Ala may cause a weak dominant negative effect (Figure 5C–E).
evidence: This is inferred from the comparison of phenotypes shown in Figure 5C-E.

claim: The conserved IDA C-terminus plays a role in the control of floral abscission.
source: In agreement with our structures and biochemical assays, this experiment suggests a role of the conserved IDA C-terminus in the control of floral abscission.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined structural, biochemical, and genetic data.

claim: Plant LRR-RKs harbor spiral-shaped ectodomains and require shape-complementary co-receptor proteins for receptor activation.
source: In contrast to animal LRR receptors, plant LRR-RKs harbor spiral-shaped ectodomains and thus they require shape-complementary co-receptor proteins for receptor activation (Hothorn et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: For a rapidly growing number of plant signaling pathways, SERK proteins act as essential co-receptors.
source: For a rapidly growing number of plant signaling pathways, SERK proteins act as these essential co-receptors (Wang et al., 2015; Meng et al., 2015; Meng et al., 2016; Brandt and Hothorn, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent work.

claim: SERK1 has been previously reported as a positive regulator in plant embryogenesis.
source: SERK1 has been previously reported as a positive regulator in plant embryogenesis (Hecht et al., 2001; Salaj et al., 2008), male sporogenesis (Albrecht et al., 2005; Colcombet et al., 2005), brassinosteroid signaling (Albrecht et al., 2008; Gou et al., 2012; Santiago et al., 2013) and in phytosulfokine perception (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SERK1 has been previously reported as a positive regulator in male sporogenesis.
source: SERK1 has been previously reported as a positive regulator in plant embryogenesis (Hecht et al., 2001; Salaj et al., 2008), male sporogenesis (Albrecht et al., 2005; Colcombet et al., 2005), brassinosteroid signaling (Albrecht et al., 2008; Gou et al., 2012; Santiago et al., 2013) and in phytosulfokine perception (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

source: SERK1 has been previously reported as a positive regulator in plant embryogenesis (Hecht et al., 2001; Salaj et al., 2008), male sporogenesis (Albrecht et al., 2005; Colcombet et al., 2005), brassinosteroid signaling (Albrecht et al., 2008; Gou et al., 2012; Santiago et al., 2013) and in phytosulfokine perception (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

source: SERK1 has been previously reported as a positive regulator in plant embryogenesis (Hecht et al., 2001; Salaj et al., 2008), male sporogenesis (Albrecht et al., 2005; Colcombet et al., 2005), brassinosteroid signaling (Albrecht et al., 2008; Gou et al., 2012; Santiago et al., 2013) and in phytosulfokine perception (Wang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Recent findings support a positive role for SERK1 in floral abscission.
source: Recent findings by Meng et al., 2016 and our mechanistic studies now also support a positive role for SERK1 in floral abscission.
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work and the data presented in this study.

claim: serk1-1 mutant plants show intermediate abscission phenotypes when compared to haesa/hsl2 mutants.
source: As serk1-1 mutant plants show intermediate abscission phenotypes when compared to haesa/hsl2 mutants, SERK1 likely acts redundantly with other SERKs in the abscission zone (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by petal break-strength assay data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: SERK1 likely acts redundantly with other SERKs in the abscission zone.
source: As serk1-1 mutant plants show intermediate abscission phenotypes when compared to haesa/hsl2 mutants, SERK1 likely acts redundantly with other SERKs in the abscission zone (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is inferred from the intermediate phenotype of serk1-1 mutants.

claim: It has been previously suggested that SERK1 can inhibit cell separation.
source: It has been previously suggested that SERK1 can inhibit cell separation (Lewis et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: SERK1 can activate cell separation upon IDA sensing.
source: However our results show that SERK1 also can activate this process upon IDA sensing, indicating that SERKs may fulfill several different functions in the course of the abscission process.
evidence: This is supported by the data presented in this study.

claim: SERKs may fulfill several different functions in the course of the abscission process.
source: However our results show that SERK1 also can activate this process upon IDA sensing, indicating that SERKs may fulfill several different functions in the course of the abscission process.
evidence: This is inferred from the dual roles of SERK1 in activating and potentially inhibiting cell separation.

claim: The sequence of the mature IDA peptide has not been experimentally determined in planta.
source: While the sequence of the mature IDA peptide has not been experimentally determined in planta (Stenvik et al., 2008), our HAESA-IDA complex structures and calorimetry assays suggest that active IDLs are hydroxyprolinated dodecamers.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Active IDLs are hydroxyprolinated dodecamers.
source: While the sequence of the mature IDA peptide has not been experimentally determined in planta (Stenvik et al., 2008), our HAESA-IDA complex structures and calorimetry assays suggest that active IDLs are hydroxyprolinated dodecamers.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural and biochemical data presented in the study.

claim: Proteolytic processing of full-length IDA in vivo may be regulated in a cell-type or tissue-specific manner.
source: It will be thus interesting to see if proteolytic processing of full-length IDA in vivo is regulated in a cell-type or tissue-specific manner.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.

claim: The central Hyp residue in IDA is found buried in the HAESA peptide binding surface.
source: The central Hyp residue in IDA is found buried in the HAESA peptide binding surface and thus this post-translational modification may regulate IDA bioactivity.
evidence: This is supported by structural data.

claim: The post-translational modification of the central Hyp residue may regulate IDA bioactivity.
source: The central Hyp residue in IDA is found buried in the HAESA peptide binding surface and thus this post-translational modification may regulate IDA bioactivity.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural observation and biochemical data.

claim: IDLs share a common receptor binding mode.
source: Our comparative structural and biochemical analysis further suggests that IDLs share a common receptor binding mode, but may preferably bind to HAESA, HSL1 or HSL2 in different plant tissues and organs.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural comparison of IDA and IDL1 binding to HAESA.

claim: IDLs may preferably bind to HAESA, HSL1 or HSL2 in different plant tissues and organs.
source: Our comparative structural and biochemical analysis further suggests that IDLs share a common receptor binding mode, but may preferably bind to HAESA, HSL1 or HSL2 in different plant tissues and organs.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the structural and biochemical data.

claim: The presence of SERK1 dramatically increases the HAESA binding specificity and affinity for IDA.
source: In our quantitative biochemical assays, the presence of SERK1 dramatically increases the HAESA binding specificity and affinity for IDA.
evidence: This is supported by ITC data.

claim: Receptor and co-receptor together form the IDA binding pocket.
source: This observation is consistent with our complex structure in which receptor and co-receptor together form the IDA binding pocket.
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data.

claim: SERK1 specifically interacts with the very C-terminus of IDLs.
source: The fact that SERK1 specifically interacts with the very C-terminus of IDLs may allow for the rational design of peptide hormone antagonists, as previously demonstrated for the brassinosteroid pathway (Muto and Todoroki, 2013; Santiago et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data.

claim: The interaction of SERK1 with the C-terminus of IDLs may allow for the rational design of peptide hormone antagonists.
source: The fact that SERK1 specifically interacts with the very C-terminus of IDLs may allow for the rational design of peptide hormone antagonists, as previously demonstrated for the brassinosteroid pathway (Muto and Todoroki, 2013; Santiago et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the structural data and supported by citations to similar work in other systems.

claim: The SERK1 ectodomain binds HAESA with nanomolar affinity, but only in the presence of IDA.
source: Importantly, our calorimetry assays reveal that the SERK1 ectodomain binds HAESA with nanomolar affinity, but only in the presence of IDA (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by ITC data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Ligand-induced formation of a receptor – co-receptor complex may allow the HAESA and SERK1 kinase domains to efficiently trans-phosphorylate and activate each other in the cytoplasm.
source: This ligand-induced formation of a receptor – co-receptor complex may allow the HAESA and SERK1 kinase domains to efficiently trans-phosphorylate and activate each other in the cytoplasm.
evidence: This is inferred from the ITC data and in vitro kinase assays.

claim: The reported binding affinities for IDA and SERK1 might differ in the context of the full-length, membrane-embedded signaling complex.
source: It is of note that our reported binding affinities for IDA and SERK1 have been measured using synthetic peptides and the isolated HAESA and SERK1 ectodomains, and thus might differ in the context of the full-length, membrane-embedded signaling complex.
evidence: This is a cautionary note about the interpretation of the in vitro binding data.

claim: The HAESA – IDA – SERK1 structure reveals an overall conserved mode of SERK1 binding compared to the brassinosteroid receptor signaling complex.
source: Comparison of our HAESA – IDA – SERK1 structure with the brassinosteroid receptor signaling complex, where SERK1 also acts as co-receptor (Santiago et al., 2013), reveals an overall conserved mode of SERK1 binding, while the ligand binding pockets map to very different areas in the corresponding receptors (LRRs 2 – 14; HAESA; LRRs 21 – 25, BRI1) and may involve an island domain (BRI1) or not (HAESA) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 6A and citation.

claim: The ligand binding pockets map to very different areas in HAESA and BRI1 receptors.
source: Comparison of our HAESA – IDA – SERK1 structure with the brassinosteroid receptor signaling complex, where SERK1 also acts as co-receptor (Santiago et al., 2013), reveals an overall conserved mode of SERK1 binding, while the ligand binding pockets map to very different areas in the corresponding receptors (LRRs 2 – 14; HAESA; LRRs 21 – 25, BRI1) and may involve an island domain (BRI1) or not (HAESA) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Several residues in the SERK1 N-terminal capping domain and the LRR inner surface contribute to the formation of both HAESA-IDA-SERK1 and BRI1-brassinolide-SERK1 complexes.
source: Several residues in the SERK1 N-terminal capping domain (Thr59SERK1, Phe61SERK1) and the LRR inner surface (Asp75SERK1, Tyr101SERK1, SER121SERK1, Phe145SERK1) contribute to the formation of both complexes (Figures 4C,D, 6B) (Santiago et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by structural comparison shown in Figures 4C, 4D, and 6B, and citation.

claim: Residues 53-55SERK1 from the SERK1 N-terminal cap mediate specific interactions with the IDA peptide.
source: In addition, residues 53-55SERK1 from the SERK1 N-terminal cap mediate specific interactions with the IDA peptide (Figures 4C, 6B).
evidence: This is supported by crystal structure data shown in Figures 4C and 6B.

claim: Residues 53-55SERK1 are not involved in the sensing of the steroid hormone brassinolide.
source: These residues are not involved in the sensing of the steroid hormone brassinolide (Santiago et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The co-receptor completes the hormone binding pocket in both HAESA-IDA and BRI1-brassinolide complexes.
source: In both cases however, the co-receptor completes the hormone binding pocket.
evidence: This is supported by structural data from both complexes.

claim: SERK1 may promote high-affinity peptide hormone and brassinosteroid sensing by slowing down dissociation of the ligand from its cognate receptor.
source: This fact together with the largely overlapping SERK1 binding surfaces in HAESA and BRI1 allows us to speculate that SERK1 may promote high-affinity peptide hormone and brassinosteroid sensing by simply slowing down dissociation of the ligand from its cognate receptor.
evidence: This is a speculative statement based on the structural comparison.

claim: The HAESA ectodomain (residues 20–620) was purified from baculovirus-infected insect cells.
source: We purified the HAESA ectodomain (residues 20–620) from baculovirus-infected insect cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, see Materials and methods) and quantified the interaction of the ~75 kDa glycoprotein with synthetic IDA peptides using isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used.

claim: About 0.2 mg of purified HAESA and 0.1 mg of purified SERK1 protein were obtained from 1 L of insect cell culture, respectively.
source: About 0.2 mg of purified HAESA and 0.1 mg of purified SERK1 protein were obtained from 1 L of insect cell culture, respectively.
evidence: This is a description of the protein yield from the expression system.
